section_summary: This section documents Japanese troop movements during the Manchurian Incident from late November 1931 through January 1932, including withdrawals and advances along the Peking–Mukden Railway, the occupation of towns, railway operations, and foreign observers’ reports. From February through early March 1932, the focus shifts to the Shanghai Incident: reinforcements sent from Japan, possible operations against Nanking, landings at Woosung and Shanghai, and the deployment of multiple Japanese divisions. The papers consist mainly of State Department telegrams and docket sheets, with one consular despatch and several memorandum or cross-reference sheets.

subfiles.title: Return of Japanese military trains from the Peking–Mukden Railway
subfiles.from: Perkins, U.S. Legation at Peiping, relaying Mukden
subfiles.about: Reports that Japanese military trains dispatched over the Peking–Mukden Railway had returned.
subfiles.summary: The docket sheet identifies telegram 1022 from China. Perkins relays a brief report from Mukden stating that Japanese military trains sent over the Peking–Mukden Railway had returned; the message was repeated to the Minister at Nanking.

subfiles.title: Reported Japanese withdrawal to the Liao River
subfiles.from: Perkins, U.S. Legation at Peiping, relaying the Military Attaché at Chinchow
subfiles.about: Reports a claimed Japanese withdrawal toward the Liao River and efforts to verify it through an observer.
subfiles.summary: Chinese commander says Japanese forces withdrew to the Liao River; the Military Attaché tried to send an observer, expecting failure because communications were cut, and Mukden was asked to investigate.

subfiles.title: Japanese forces transferred east of the Liao River
subfiles.from: Perkins, U.S. Legation at Peiping, reporting Colonel Margetts
subfiles.about: Relays Lieutenant Aldrich's confirmation that nearly all Japanese forces had moved east of the Liao River.
subfiles.summary: Colonel Margetts reported that Lieutenant Aldrich reached the Liao River and found that all Japanese forces had transferred eastward except about 300 troops. Those remaining guarded Hsinmin and patrolled the railway toward Paikipu. Chinese repairs to the line between Dahushan and Hsinmin were expected shortly.

subfiles.title: League Council deliberations and military information from Manchuria
subfiles.doc_type: document file note and two-section telegram
subfiles.from: Shaw, U.S. Embassy at Paris, transmitting reports from Ambassador Dawes and Sweetser
subfiles.about: Reviews League Council negotiations and distributes Chinese, British, and French reports on Japanese and Chinese military activity.
subfiles.summary: The first section describes a pause in League Council meetings while delegates awaited Japanese and Chinese replies concerning evacuation, neutral observers, and Chinchow. The second compiles reports of Japanese aerial reconnaissance, warships and reinforcements, activity at Harbin, withdrawal to Chuliuho, and plans to return a naval landing party from Tianjin to Tanggu. French observers estimated 27,600 Chinese personnel east of the Great Wall, including about 17,000 combat troops, in dispositions resembling those before September 18.

subfiles.title: Japanese withdrawals from Hailar and Taonan and other Manchurian activity
subfiles.from: Perkins, U.S. Legation at Peiping, relaying the American Consul at Mukden
subfiles.about: Summarizes clashes, Chinese troop dispositions, and the withdrawal of most Japanese troops from the Hailar and Taonan districts.
subfiles.summary: Mukden reports Chinese activity near Qiqihar and Jehol troops at Goubangzi; Japanese withdrew most forces from quiet Hailar and Taonan into the South Manchuria Railway Zone.

subfiles.title: Japanese detachment sent to Nankai University
subfiles.from: Lockhart, U.S. Consulate at Tientsin
subfiles.to: Secretary of State and U.S. Legation at Peiping
subfiles.about: Reports the unexplained movement of a Japanese armored car, machine gun, and small detachment to Nankai University.
subfiles.summary: About fifteen or twenty Japanese soldiers accompanied an armored car and machine gun from the Japanese concession to Nankai University. The detachment remained near a hotel before returning. Lockhart viewed the movement into a previously quiet district as evidence of poor conciliation during strained relations.

subfiles.title: Observer verification of forces near Chinchow
subfiles.from: Perkins, U.S. Legation at Peiping, relaying Colonel Margetts
subfiles.about: Reports direct observation of Chinese units around Chinchow and railway repairs near Yingkou.
subfiles.summary: Observers, including the American attaché, verified the 19th and 20th Brigades and 13th Artillery near Faku; the 20th Brigade was near Chinchow, and British engineers repaired the line near Yingkou.

subfiles.title: Additional Japanese troops for Manchuria and Tientsin
subfiles.doc_type: document file note and confidential telegram
subfiles.from: Forbes, U.S. Embassy at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports Cabinet approval for Japanese reinforcements and General Staff thinking about pressure on Chinchow.
subfiles.summary: Japan's Cabinet approved about 4,000 more troops for Manchuria and 1,000 for Tianjin; Forbes told Cranford to reiterate American opposition to further military action against Chinese forces.

subfiles.title: Railway battalion sent into the Changtu–Faku region
subfiles.from: Perkins, U.S. Legation at Peiping, relaying the American Consul General at Mukden
subfiles.about: Reports the dispatch of a Japanese railway battalion against alleged bandits near Changtu and Faku.
subfiles.summary: Japanese headquarters stated that the First Railway Battalion had left Siping that morning to clear an estimated 7,000 bandits from the Changtu–Faku region. The report also notes an official reception celebrating the formation of the Provincial Government.

subfiles.title: Additional Japanese troops at Newchwang
subfiles.doc_type: document file note or cross-reference sheet
subfiles.from: Gilbert, Geneva
subfiles.about: Records a report that 500 additional Japanese troops reached Newchwang from Liaoyang.
subfiles.summary: Docket sheet for Geneva telegram 320: 500 additional Japanese troops arrived at Newchwang from Liaoyang; telegram not present.

subfiles.title: Expected arrival of 1,700 Japanese troops at Tientsin
subfiles.from: Lockhart, U.S. Consulate at Tientsin
subfiles.to: Secretary of State and U.S. Legation at Peiping
subfiles.about: Reports that 1,700 Japanese troops were scheduled to arrive at Tientsin on December 26 and 27.
subfiles.summary: Japanese headquarters announced the impending arrival of 1,700 troops, including an artillery company with four field pieces, as a precautionary measure. Local observers believed the deployment presaged an attack on Chinchow within a week. Lockhart warned that the influx would greatly alarm the Chinese population.

subfiles.title: Japanese brigade advancing from Yingkou toward Panshan
subfiles.from: Johnson, U.S. Legation at Peiping, relaying the American Consul General at Mukden
subfiles.about: Reports a Japanese brigade crossing near Yingkou and marching through Tianzhuangtai toward Panshan.
subfiles.summary: A Japanese brigade with cavalry and artillery crossed the river at Yingkou, moved to Tianzhuangtai, and continued toward Panshan. Troops previously dispatched westward against bandits had returned to Liaoyang and Yingkou. Aircraft also departed Mukden in a westerly direction.

subfiles.title: Japanese attack and troop concentration at Dawa
subfiles.from: Johnson, U.S. Legation at Peiping, relaying the Military Attaché at Chinchow
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese aircraft and ground forces engaging a Chinese armored train at Dawa.
subfiles.summary: Chinese headquarters observed Japanese aircraft and a combined force south of Dawa; six bombs missed a Chinese armored train, which returned fire, and 400 Japanese cavalry were on the flank.

subfiles.title: Capture of Panshan and troop trains from Mukden
subfiles.from: Johnson, U.S. Legation at Peiping, relaying the American Consul General at Mukden
subfiles.about: Reports the capture of Panshan and extensive Japanese troop-train activity along the Peking–Mukden Railway.
subfiles.summary: Japanese forces reportedly captured Panshan and continued toward Goubangzi. Nine additional troop trains departed Mukden after midnight, while nine earlier trains unloaded at Hsinmin and returned. The operation appeared intended at least to suppress bandits in the triangle between the Liao River and the railway.

subfiles.title: Japanese troops and equipment leaving Mukden
subfiles.from: Johnson, U.S. Legation at Peiping, relaying the American Consul General at Mukden
subfiles.about: Reports large troop trains departing Mukden and Japanese brigades moving westward.
subfiles.summary: Four trains of twenty-nine cars each carried Japanese troops and equipment from Mukden over the Peking–Mukden Railway. The Murai Brigade had arrived at Mukden, while General Tamon's brigade was reportedly moving west along the Goubangzi–Yingkou Railway.

subfiles.title: Tamon Division advance toward Goubangzi
subfiles.from: Johnson, U.S. Legation at Peiping, relaying the American Consul General at Mukden
subfiles.about: Reports the continued Japanese advance beyond Panshan and the dispatch of additional trains from Mukden.
subfiles.summary: Japanese headquarters placed the Tamon Division eight miles northwest of Panshan. Troops advancing along the Peking–Mukden Railway had reached a wrecked bridge just east of Goubangzi, where repairs were nearly complete. Six more trains of troops left Mukden that afternoon.

subfiles.title: Disposition of Japanese troops in Manchuria
subfiles.from: M. S. Myers, American Consul General at Mukden
subfiles.to: Secretary of State; enclosure addressed to Nelson Trusler Johnson, American Minister at Peiping
subfiles.about: Transmits a military attaché's estimate of Japanese troop dispositions and railway-guard deployments in Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: Myers forwards a memorandum based on information supplied by Lieutenant Colonel McIlroy after his return from Qiqihar. It describes Japanese troop locations and notes that independent railway-guard battalions had been placed on lines beyond the South Manchuria Railway itself. The enclosed table estimates that Japan had slightly fewer than 30,000 men in Manchuria, with replacements likely raising the total above that figure.

subfiles.title: Japanese activity in the Qinhuangdao–Shanhaiguan area
subfiles.from: Lockhart, U.S. Consulate at Tientsin
subfiles.to: Secretary of State and U.S. Legation at Peiping
subfiles.about: Reports bridge repair, reconnaissance flights, warships, and retreating Chinese troops around Qinhuangdao.
subfiles.summary: Japanese personnel were repairing the railway bridge at Lianshan, while some Chinese troops continued moving west through Qinhuangdao. Japanese aircraft conducted reconnaissance over the Qinhuangdao–Shanhaiguan area, and several Japanese warships lay at Qinhuangdao. None of the Chinese troops retreating from Chinchow had yet reached the Tianjin area.

subfiles.title: Japanese forces at Shanhaiguan and Tientsin
subfiles.from: Lockhart, U.S. Consulate at Tientsin
subfiles.to: Secretary of State and U.S. Legation at Peiping
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese entry into Shanhaiguan and an approximately 3,000-man garrison at Tientsin.
subfiles.summary: Japanese forces advancing toward Shanhaiguan reportedly reached the city without Chinese resistance and took control of telephone and telegraph lines to the east. Japanese authorities planned a review of their Tianjin troops, then numbering about 3,000, in the Japanese concession.

subfiles.title: Japanese troops transported on Chinese trains
subfiles.doc_type: document file note or cross-reference sheet
subfiles.from: Hawkling Yen, Chinese Legation
subfiles.about: Records a Chinese Legation communication concerning Japanese troops traveling on Chinese trains.
subfiles.summary: Docket sheet for a Chinese Legation communication on Japanese troops moving on Chinese trains; communication not present.

subfiles.title: Lieutenant Brown's report on Japanese operations in Manchuria
subfiles.from: Johnson, U.S. Legation at Peiping, relaying Lieutenant Brown at Mukden
subfiles.about: Assesses Japanese troop strength, railway control, possible operations in Jehol, and the army's political attitude.
subfiles.summary: Lt. Brown estimates about 15,000 Japanese hold the Mukden-Shanhaiguan railway, with requisitions suggesting Jehol occupation or an anti-bandit campaign; officers blame Chinchow observers for guerrilla warfare.

subfiles.title: Japanese troops entrained for Suizhong
subfiles.from: Lockhart, U.S. Consulate at Tientsin
subfiles.to: Secretary of State and U.S. Legation at Peiping
subfiles.about: Reports the departure of approximately 350 Japanese troops from Tientsin to Suizhong.
subfiles.summary: Approximately 350 Japanese troops boarded trains at Tianjin for Suizhong. Japanese authorities attributed the move to improved conditions in the Tianjin–Beijing area rather than reinforcement needs. Lockhart nevertheless suggested that it might relate to operations closing on Jehol from Chinchow.

subfiles.title: Japanese deployments between Shanhaiguan and Chinchow
subfiles.from: Johnson, U.S. Legation at Peiping, summarizing Lieutenant Aldrich
subfiles.about: Summarizes Japanese withdrawals, garrisons, railway control, and naval deployments from Shanhaiguan to Chinchow.
subfiles.summary: Japanese troops pulled back toward Chinchow as Chinese cavalry threatened Peipiao; Japan sought Peipiao's coal and railway control, with warships at Shanhaiguan and Qinhuangdao.

subfiles.title: Japanese occupation of Tongliao
subfiles.from: Johnson, U.S. Legation at Peiping, relaying the American Consul General at Mukden
subfiles.about: Reports a Japanese battalion's occupation of Tongliao after expelling Chinese cavalry troops.
subfiles.summary: Japanese headquarters reported that a battalion occupied Tongliao on January 14 after ejecting some 3,000 alleged Chinese partisans, with sixty Chinese and no Japanese losses. Other information identified the supposed partisans as members of the Chinese Third Cavalry Brigade, about 1,000 of whom had been in the town.

subfiles.title: Prospect of Japanese military operations against Nanking
subfiles.doc_type: document file note and confidential telegram
subfiles.from: Peck, U.S. mission at Nanking
subfiles.about: Warns that Nanking might enter the field of operations and cites a report that a Japanese division was bound for Shanghai or Nanking.
subfiles.summary: Peck expects Nanking to be drawn into operations given ten Japanese naval vessels, and Tokyo learned a whole Japanese division was bound for Shanghai or Nanking.

subfiles.title: Admiral Toyoda's account of the Shanghai fighting
subfiles.from: Forbes, U.S. Embassy at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Records Admiral Toyoda's explanation of the Shanghai incident and the intended employment and landing of Japanese reinforcements.
subfiles.summary: Admiral Toyoda calls the Shanghai fighting an unexpected Chinese attack, admits civilian atrocities, and says incoming Japanese land forces will stay defensive and relieve marines, landing in the Settlement if the river is clear.

subfiles.title: Request for Japanese troops at Harbin
subfiles.doc_type: document file note and confidential telegram
subfiles.from: Hanson, U.S. Consulate at Harbin
subfiles.about: Reports Ohashi's request for troops from Changchun and warns that their arrival could provoke looting in Harbin.
subfiles.summary: Ohashi privately informed the American, British, and French representatives that he had independently requested Japanese troops from Changchun. Hanson believed conditions did not justify the request. He feared that Chinese troops retreating before a Japanese advance might loot foreign property in Harbin.

subfiles.title: Landing of Japanese land forces at Woosung
subfiles.from: William R. Castle Jr., Undersecretary of State
subfiles.about: Records a memorandum concerning the first landing of Japanese army forces at Woosung on February 7.
subfiles.summary: Docket sheet for Castle's memorandum on the first Japanese land force landing at Woosung on February 7; memorandum not present.

subfiles.title: Colonel McIlroy's estimate of Japanese troops for Shanghai
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Records McIlroy's estimate that incoming advance troops would bring Japanese strength at Shanghai to about 10,000.
subfiles.summary: Docket sheet: Colonel McIlroy's February 6 report expects advance troops at Shanghai around February 8-9, raising Japanese strength to about 10,000; text absent.

subfiles.title: Japanese troops reported as having left Japan
subfiles.from: Miller, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Records a memorandum based on Colonel Washizu's statement about Japanese troops that had departed Japan.
subfiles.summary: Docket sheet for Miller's memorandum on Japanese troop departures per Colonel Washizu; no troop list appears.

subfiles.title: Decision to send the Japanese 11th Division to Shanghai
subfiles.doc_type: document file note or cross-reference sheet
subfiles.from: U.S. Embassy in Japan
subfiles.about: Records a telegram concerning the decision to dispatch the Japanese 11th Division to Shanghai.
subfiles.summary: Docket sheet for telegram 74: decision to send Japan's 11th Division to Shanghai; telegram not present.

subfiles.title: War Office announcement of additional divisions for Shanghai
subfiles.from: Forbes, U.S. Embassy at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports that two more Japanese divisions would go to Shanghai and that a third might follow.
subfiles.summary: Forbes reports rumors of a grave crisis and coalition cabinet; the War Office announced two more divisions for Shanghai, perhaps a third, amid strict press censorship.

subfiles.title: Captain Mayer's report on military operations around Shanghai
subfiles.from: Cunningham, U.S. Consulate at Shanghai, relaying Captain Mayer
subfiles.to: Secretary of State and War Department
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese replacements, the occupation of Jiangwan, supply arrangements, casualties, and Chinese troop deployments.
subfiles.summary: Captain Mayer reports 400 replacements for the 24th Brigade landed, Japan claims occupation of Jiangwan with about 1,100 casualties, and the 11th Division's whereabouts are uncertain.

subfiles.title: Reuters report of a Japanese army corps for Shanghai
subfiles.doc_type: document file note and telegram quoting a press report
subfiles.from: Perkins, U.S. Legation at Peiping, forwarding Reuters from Shanghai
subfiles.about: Forwards a report that two Japanese divisions were en route to Shanghai and three more were mobilizing in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Perkins forwards a Reuters report from Shanghai stating that a Japanese army corps would soon take the field. A source described as very reliable said that two divisions were already traveling to Shanghai and three additional divisions were being mobilized in Japan.

subfiles.title: Shanghai situation and arrival of part of the 14th Division
subfiles.from: Cunningham, U.S. Consulate at Shanghai
subfiles.about: Reports a lull in fighting, the landing of 14th Division troops, Japanese propaganda, and access controls in Zhabei.
subfiles.summary: Shanghai fronts quiet three days; about 1,500 of the 14th Division landed, General Shirakawa issued a proclamation, peace talks are deadlocked, and Japanese naval headquarters regulates access to Zhabei.
